title: Touching the earth
hook: Mara asks who witnesses his right to that seat; he touches the ground, and the earth answers

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mara: the tempter whose storms and weapons fell as flowers. Your line was the arrows become flowers. What attacked your quiet, and did you name it? Day fifty-three.

Have you ever been asked, out loud, what gives you the right? What makes you think you can do this job, hold this opinion, take up this space? It's one of the oldest weapons there is. It doesn't hurt the body. It goes straight for the sense of whether you belong. Mara's army has failed. The rocks and arrows have fallen as flowers. So Mara tries something else. He stops attacking and starts arguing. This seat, he says, belongs to me. Who are you to sit there? And his whole army roars behind him: we are his witnesses! Now, who is yours? Today, touching the earth.
screen: `WHAT GIVES YOU THE RIGHT?` → `THIS SEAT BELONGS TO ME.` → `WHO IS YOUR WITNESS?`

segments.voice: It's a good question, and it's a lonely one. Mara has a whole army to speak for him. The wanderer is alone under a tree at night, with no one there to vouch for him. In the telling, he answers that there's no living being present to be his witness. But across countless lives, he says, he has given and given, practicing generosity and patience again and again. And then he moves his right hand. He draws it out from his lap, lets it rest over his right knee, and touches the ground with his fingertips. The earth itself will speak for him. And the earth answers, the telling says, with a roar like thunder: I am his witness. Mara's elephant kneels. The army scatters. In Southeast Asia there's a beloved addition: the earth appears as a goddess, and she wrings out her long hair, and from it pours all the water of his past good deeds, a flood that sweeps Mara's army away. You'll see her in temples in Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar. And the gesture is everywhere. Look at almost any seated Buddha statue and check the right hand. If it's reaching down to touch the ground, that's this moment. It's called the earth-touching gesture, and it may be the most common pose in all of Buddhist art. What does it teach? When someone asks what gives you the right, you don't have to shout louder. You can put your hand on the ground. The earth under you, and the good you've actually done, is witness enough.
screen: `NO ONE HERE TO SPEAK FOR HIM.` · `HIS HAND REACHES TO THE GROUND.` · `THE EARTH ROARS: I AM HIS WITNESS.` · `THE MOST COMMON POSE IN ART.` · then, large: `THE EARTH IS YOUR WITNESS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Now reach down and touch the ground with your right hand: the floor, the grass, the carpet. If you can't reach, press your feet firmly into the floor instead. Feel it: solid, holding you up, asking nothing. Bring to mind one good thing you have actually done. Small is fine. A kindness, an honest word, a promise kept. Let the ground and that memory be your witnesses. You don't need anyone else to vouch for you right now. Stay with the touch, and the breath. The bell holds the time.
Touching the earth. The wanderer's right hand reaching down to call the earth as his witness, the gesture on countless Buddha statues.
Your line: the earth is your witness. Today, when you doubt your right to be where you are, press your feet into the ground and remember one good thing you've done. Day fifty-three.

howItsDone: The earth-touching gesture (bhumisparsha mudra) is one of the most common poses in Buddhist statues, and in Southeast Asia many temples honor the earth goddess who wrings the waters of merit from her hair.

touch the ground and let the earth answer.

original.note: Sanskrit: earth-touching, as in bhūmisparśa mudrā, the earth-witness gesture.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha statue is just resting its hand on its knee.
what it means: the hand reaches down to call the earth as witness to his right to the seat of awakening.

what a scholar hears: the Nidanakatha has the earth roar in witness to his past generosity (as Vessantara); the earth goddess (Thai Mae Thorani) wringing her hair is a later Southeast Asian development.

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): Mara's claim and the earth as witness

notes: In the Nidanakatha he cites his great gifts as Vessantara; the script generalizes to 'across countless lives he has given'. Confirm.
The earth goddess (Thai Mae Thorani / Phra Mae Thorani; Khmer Neang Konghing; Burmese Wathondaye) wringing her hair: Southeast Asian tradition, not in the Pali canon. Confirm countries named.
'May be the most common pose in all of Buddhist art': hedged; confirm or soften further.
